title: Two Hundred Fans and One Wet Summer
paragraphs: A workshop near Zengcheng makes palm-leaf fans, the kind older people use on a hot evening. It sells about 200 a summer at sixty yuan each, and an electric fan costs 120 yuan and lasts five years. The workshop has seven workers, and the youngest of them is fifty-six years old now.

The leaves are cut in October, boiled, bleached in the sun for nine days and pressed flat. A fan takes four days and needs a frame of thin bamboo, which is split by hand. In July the workshop found 70 finished fans with grey-green mould along the edge, after three weeks of rain.

Mould cannot be washed off a palm leaf, so the workers wiped each fan with a dry cloth. Two days in the sun left pale marks on 22 of them, and those were sold at twenty yuan. The rest went back into boxes with a small bag of drying powder that costs four yuan.

Ms Zhou, who is sixty-four and has made fans for forty years, said this was the wettest summer. "A fan is a dry thing, and it lives in the hand, not in a box," she said. "A box in this weather is a small garden," she added, and the workshop lost about 2,900 yuan.

In August it bought a dehumidifier for 2,400 yuan, and the store room now holds 300 fans. The humidity stays at about 55 percent, which is what a dried palm leaf needs. A tea house ordered forty fans to hang on its wall, and they are the first fans nobody will use.

title: Seven Puppets That Would Not Dry
paragraphs: A shadow puppet workshop in Luogang makes its figures from donkey hide, which is scraped thin. The hide must dry in the shade for three days, and each skin takes four days of work. In June a wet week stopped the drying, and seven of the twelve skins went bad.

The workshop tried to hurry, and it put three skins near a heater to dry them. The edges curled like dry leaves, so those three were lost as well, and the workshop stopped. "You see water on the skin and you think of fire, but the skin thinks of its own shape," Mr Wu said.

The lost skins cost about 2,000 yuan, but the order they belonged to was worth much more. A cultural centre had ordered six sets for a spring show, at 2,800 yuan a set, for 20 June. The workshop delivered four sets and asked for two more weeks on the other two.

The centre agreed, on condition that the two sets came with a short talk for school groups. Mr Wu said yes, then spent a week learning what to say and when to stop. The talk is now twelve minutes long, and it begins with a piece of hide, not a finished puppet.

In July the workshop built a drying room for 5,000 yuan, with a fan and two gauges. Skins now dry in four days, whatever the weather, and none have been lost since. Mr Wu has raised his price to 3,100 yuan a set, and the centre has ordered four more.

title: The Silver That Turned Black in a Week
paragraphs: In February, a silver workshop in Liwan made 40 bracelets from a new batch of alloy. Within a week, twelve came back black, and the shops that sold them asked why. The alloy held more copper than the supplier's sheet promised, and the copper had reacted with the air.

The owner, Ms Yan, used to test each batch the way her father taught her, with a drop of liquid. The drop turns dark red when copper is present, and she had never seen it in her shop. She had not tested the new batch, because the supplier had sent the same sheet for eleven years.

Taking back twelve bracelets cost 9,000 yuan, and two of the three shops stopped ordering. The supplier said the batch had been mixed at another factory and offered to replace it. Ms Yan refused the replacement and asked for her money back instead, which took three weeks.

She spent 400 yuan on a testing kit and now tests every batch before it is cut. The test takes twenty minutes and one gram of metal, and she writes the result in a book. The workshop has gone back to its old supplier, whose price has risen by eight percent since 2023.

The bracelets that came back were melted down, and eleven of the twelve are now in the shops. The twelfth had a name cut into it, so the workshop made a new one for that customer. Ms Yan keeps the blackened piece in a drawer by the door, where the light can reach it.

title: Sixty Umbrellas That Would Not Open
paragraphs: A workshop in a town near Huadu has made oil-paper umbrellas by hand since 1978. In April it finished 60 that would not open, because the bamboo ribs split at the fold. The ribs had been cut from young stems that still held water, and the fault showed only at the end.

Each umbrella has 32 ribs, a bamboo handle, a paper skin and three coats of tung oil. It takes six days of work and sells for 85 yuan, and the oil alone costs nine. The workshop buys bamboo from one grower, who cuts stems at least four years old and dries them for six months.

That spring the grower's field was damaged by wind, so the workshop bought 300 stems from another seller. The stems looked the same, but they were two years younger and still held water inside. Nine umbrellas tore when the workers tried to open them, and the other 51 stayed shut.

Mr Huang, who has made umbrellas for thirty-one years, said the fault appeared only after the oil. "Young bamboo is soft, and the oil makes it stiffer than it can bear," he said. The workshop replaced 1,920 ribs and lost three weeks of work before the order was ready.

The museum shop waited and took 20 umbrellas in May, at the old price of 85 yuan. The workshop now writes the year the bamboo was cut on the inside of each handle. It also keeps 200 dry stems, so the next mistake will cost a day rather than a month.

title: The Tap That Filled a Bucket Overnight
paragraphs: On 12 March, a grade 8 class at a middle school in Tianhe put a plastic bucket under a leaking tap in the toilet block and left it there for a full day. In the morning the bucket held 4.6 litres, enough for nine large bottles.

The class had walked past that tap for months, and nobody thought a slow drip mattered, because the sound was soft and the water vanished into the drain. Their teacher, Ms Qiu, asked them to measure it instead of arguing about a repair.

They counted 41 drops in one minute, which works out at 4.6 litres a day and about 138 litres in a month. A check of the whole building then found nine taps dripping in the same way, two of them in the staff room.

The repair took one afternoon and cost 280 yuan for new washers, paid from a fund for small repairs. The school had delayed it because the water bill comes once a term and nobody looks at a single tap. "We were not careless," said the caretaker, Mr Kong. "We just never had a number."

In April the class measured again and found the nine taps had been losing about 1,240 litres a month, close to what a small family uses. The figure is now written above each tap, with one line under it: one drip, one bucket a day.

In June the school added a line to the monthly cleaning list: check every tap on the first Monday. New students still ask about the card, and Ms Qiu lets the class explain the bucket, the drops and the 138 litres themselves.

title: Four Degrees Between Two Classrooms
paragraphs: For one week in November, two grade 8 classes at a school in Yuexiu hung thermometers at the same height and read them three times a day. By Friday one room was 3.9 degrees warmer than the other, and neither class believed it at first.

The rooms hold almost the same number of students, 46 and 45, and they share a wall, so both classes expected the readings to match. The difference turned out to be the windows: one room has a wall of glass facing west.

The gap was clearest at three in the afternoon, when the sun reached the glass. On sunny days the warm room hit 29.6 degrees while the other stayed at 25.7, and on cloudy days the gap fell to 0.8 degrees.

The class took the numbers to the school office and asked for blinds, and the first answer was no, because 2,300 yuan was not in the year's plan. A parent at a factory that makes blinds offered the material, so the school paid only for fittings.

The blinds went up in the first week of December, and a second week of readings showed the gap at 1.1 degrees on sunny afternoons. Students in the warm room also stopped opening the door to cool it, which had made the corridor cold.

"We stopped guessing," said their teacher, Ms Xia. "The thermometer did the talking, and the office listened to it faster than it listened to us." The class now lends the thermometers to other rooms and keeps a small chart in the corridor.

title: Forty-Seven Kilograms in One Bin
paragraphs: In the last week of September, students at a middle school in Panyu weighed every plate left on the tables in the canteen. They used two kitchen scales and one notebook, and the total for five days came to 236 kilograms of food.

About 600 students eat lunch at the school, so the waste worked out at 47 kilograms a day, or roughly 80 grams per student. Over a 200-day school year that is more than nine tonnes, enough to fill a small truck twice over.

The students then looked inside the bins on three separate days and wrote down what they saw. Rice made up about half the weight, whole buns came next, and many students said the rice portion was simply too large for them to finish.

In November the canteen tried smaller rice bowls and let students ask for a second bowl for free. Waste fell by 22 percent in three weeks, the bowls cost about 1,600 yuan, and the kitchen saved more than that in rice before the term ended.

Not everyone was pleased with the change. Some older students said the small bowls made lunch feel like a test, and a few took two bowls and left the second one on the table. The group still weighs every Friday, rain or shine.

The next step is a table by the door where students can leave unopened buns for anyone who wants one. The canteen has agreed to try it for two weeks in April, with a sign and one member of the group standing beside it.

title: Seventy-One Degrees on the Roof of a Bus
paragraphs: On a July afternoon, six students from a school in Baiyun stood at a bus stop with an infrared thermometer and measured the roof of a parked bus. The metal read 71 degrees, while the air around them was 34.

They had borrowed the thermometer from the physics lab and spent two weeks learning how to use it properly. The plan was to compare four surfaces in the same sun: the bus roof, the asphalt road, a metal bench and the grass in a small park.

The results were uneven: asphalt reached 63 degrees, the bench 58, and the grass stayed at 33. The bus roof was hottest because it is dark and flat, and because the air under it cannot move, so the seats inside were 46 degrees.

The students sent a one-page report to the bus company. An engineer wrote back to say the company had already tried white paint on two buses. That lowered the roof by about 9 degrees, but the paint peeled off after four months.

In September the company painted three more roofs and agreed to park buses in shade where possible. The students now measure the roofs once a month and add each new number to the report, which the engineer says he keeps on his desk.

The six students also measured their own classroom roof, which read 64 degrees and has no shade at all. The school is considering a light-coloured cover for one section, but the cost of about 8,000 yuan has not been approved.

title: The Loudest Place Was Not the Road
paragraphs: Over three afternoons in October, a group of students from a school in Haizhu made a noise map of the streets around their gate. They took readings at twelve points and wrote each number on a printed map of the area.

They expected the road to be loudest, and it measured 76 decibels at half past four, when parents park and wait. But the covered walkway inside the gate reached 84 decibels, higher than the traffic, and it was full of students at the same time.

The map showed why: the walkway has a metal roof and a tiled floor, and the sound of 200 students talking bounced between the two. The quietest place was a small garden behind the office, at 46 decibels, where almost nobody goes.

The group asked the school to move the afternoon meeting point into the garden, and the school refused at first. The garden has one narrow path, and the walkway is the only covered place on rainy days, when 200 students need somewhere to stand.

The compromise was a second meeting point under the trees, used on dry days. Readings in December showed 79 decibels in the walkway, still loud but lower than before, and the garden stayed at 46 because nothing had changed there.

A grade 8 student said she had never noticed the noise until she saw it drawn on a map. The group has since lent its meter to two other schools and put a copy of the map on the wall of the science room.

title: The Fridge That Beat Twelve Fans
paragraphs: In May, a science club at a school in Liwan borrowed a plug-in electricity meter and measured one appliance each day for two weeks. The aim was simple: find out which machine used the most power in the whole building.

The answer was not the fans, and the club checked the meter twice before believing it. One drinks fridge in the canteen used 4.1 kilowatt-hours a day, more than the twelve classroom fans together at 3.4, and it stood beside a hot oven.

The fridge was eleven years old and its door seal was torn. The club asked the caretaker to confirm the reading, and he said nobody had measured the fridge in eleven years. It had always seemed to work, so no one had asked a question about it.

The school moved the fridge in June and replaced the seal in July for 90 yuan. In September the same meter showed 2.6 kilowatt-hours a day, which comes to about 300 yuan a year, more than the club expected to save from one small repair.

The club now keeps a chart on the lab wall with the readings of five appliances, and two other schools have asked to borrow the meter. The club has written a one-page guide on how to use it without touching the wires.

The canteen manager has asked for a second measurement in summer, when the fridge works harder and the oven runs longer. "We will do it in the first week of July," said Ms Feng, the teacher who runs the club. "The number may be worse."

title: The Flagpole That Was Shorter Than Its Sign
paragraphs: A brass sign beside the flagpole of a school in Nansha says that the pole is 13.5 metres tall. In October, a grade 8 class measured it with a one-metre stick and a long shadow, and got 12.1 metres instead.

The method is old and simple, and it needs only a stick, a tape and a sunny morning. At ten they stood the stick upright and measured its shadow at 0.78 metres, while the shadow of the pole reached 9.4 metres. The pole must be 9.4 divided by 0.78.

They measured again on two other mornings and got 12.0 and 12.2 metres. A caretaker who has worked at the school for nineteen years said the pole had never been changed, and that the sign came from a builder's list rather than a measurement.

The class wrote to the school office with the numbers and a drawing of the method. The office checked with a long tape from a ladder, which is difficult and slightly unsafe, and got 12.1 metres, so the sign had been wrong by 1.4 metres for years.

A new sign was ordered in December for 60 yuan, and the old one was kept in the physics lab as a teaching object. "A number on a wall feels true," said the teacher, Mr Gao. "This one had been copied for years without anyone checking it."

The class has since measured two other poles on the playground and found one more wrong sign. It said 8 metres, and the pole is 7.3. The school has ordered a replacement, and the class keeps a list of every number it has checked.

title: Three Hundred and Forty Metres to the Classroom
paragraphs: The school map given to new students in Zengcheng says the walk from the front gate to the grade 8 building is about 200 metres. Four students walked the route with a step counter in September and got 548 steps instead.

First they measured their own step length, walking ten steps along a tape three times and taking the average, which came to 0.62 metres. Then 548 steps gave 340 metres, or 140 metres more than the map had claimed for years.

The group then counted a normal school day. From the gate to the classroom, to the canteen, to the playground and back, one student walked about 2.7 kilometres inside the school. On rainy days the route is longer, because two paths close.

The map, it turned out, was drawn by a teacher in 2016 who measured with a ruler on a satellite picture and did not include the stairs. The school printed a new map in November, and the walk now reads 340 metres with a note about the stairs.

The group has also timed the walk, which takes four minutes at a normal pace and six when the corridor is full. The school is using that figure to decide when the grade 8 classes should leave for the field on competition days.

A boy in the group said he used to think he was slow, and now he knows that the walk is long. The group plans to measure the route to the sports field next term, and has asked for a proper measuring wheel instead of a step counter.

title: Thirty-Eight Millimetres at School, Twenty-Four in the App
paragraphs: A rain gauge on the roof of a school in Huangpu collected 38 millimetres during a storm on 6 June. The weather app on three phones said 24 millimetres for the same area, and the students who read the gauge did not believe the app.

The gauge is a simple plastic tube with a scale, checked each morning by two members of the geography club. They emptied it into a measuring cup after every storm and wrote the result in a book kept on a shelf in the lab.

They checked the app again after a second storm on 21 June. The gauge showed 31 millimetres and the app showed 26. The nearest official station is six kilometres away, near the river, where summer rain is often lighter than at the school.

A teacher explained that an app reports the nearest station rather than the school roof, and that six kilometres can make a real difference in June. The club asked the district office for the station's daily figures and began comparing them every week.

Since September the club has posted its own reading on a board by the gate each morning, with the date and the time. Other classes now use it for their weather charts, and the club has written to the app company once.

The reply said that the app shows the nearest station and cannot promise local accuracy. The students have pinned that reply next to the board, under their own reading of 38 millimetres, and they do not expect the app to change.

title: One Hundred and Eighty Lux at the Back Row
paragraphs: On a cloudy morning in March, a class at a school in Huadu measured the light in their room with a small meter borrowed from the art room. The front row read 520 lux and the back row read 180.

The difference was not the lamps, which all six of them had assumed at first. The lamps were working, but two were old and dim, and the desks at the back sat under a shelf that held boxes of paper. Nobody had ever measured the room.

The class measured three rooms on the same morning, using the same meter and the same cloudy sky. The other two had a gap of about 120 lux between front and back, while theirs had 340, and the darkest corner was used for reading aloud.

The school moved the shelf into the corridor and replaced two lamps for 260 yuan. A week later the back row read 320 lux, still lower than the front but enough for reading. The class asked for one more lamp, and the school said it would decide in the summer.

The students now measure the room once a month and write the number on the board. Their teacher, Ms Wen, said the meter had turned an argument into a task, because nobody can disagree with a number that everyone in the room can see.

The class has also measured the corridor outside, which reads 90 lux in the afternoon and is used by students waiting for the bus. The school has promised a lamp there before September, and the class will measure again when it is fitted.

title: The Hundred and Twenty-Eight Who Came on Saturday
paragraphs: On a Saturday in March, 128 volunteers came to a community centre in Yuexiu to repaint a playground wall. By the tenth working day, three people were still coming, and about half of the wall was still grey.

The centre had advertised the day on a phone group and expected about thirty people. So many arrived that there were not enough brushes, and forty of them spent the morning sitting on plastic chairs while the others painted.
The paint ran out before noon, and the centre had to buy twelve more tins the same day. The organiser, Ms Ruan, had planned one big morning and had made no plan at all for the weekends that followed.

"Everyone wants to be there when it starts," she said. "Nobody signs up for the fourth Saturday, when the wall looks worse than before and the work is only sanding." The three who stayed were a retired painter, a student and a man from across the road.

They worked four hours each Saturday for six weeks. The centre paid 1,700 yuan for paint and 400 for a small scaffold, money that came from a fund for children's activities and had been meant for a trip.

The wall was finished in May, two months later than planned. The centre now asks volunteers to choose a date and a task before they arrive, and it caps each Saturday at twelve. The next project is a wooden bench, and eleven people have signed up.

title: The Bread That Came Back
paragraphs: On a Tuesday morning in April, a food bank in Baiyun refused 62 kilograms of bread donated by a bakery four streets away. The bread was still soft, but every single bag was dated three days earlier, and none of it could be given out.

Two volunteers carried the bags back to the van while the bakery manager watched. He said the bread was fine and that his own family ate bread like that at home, and he asked to speak to whoever had made the rule.

The rule came from an incident last winter, when a family received yoghurt two days out of date and a child became ill. The food bank does not give medical advice, but it decided that dated food is not worth the risk.

The argument lasted forty minutes. The manager said he would stop donating altogether, which would have cost the food bank about 90 kilograms of bread a week. A volunteer then suggested that the bakery call at nine with what was left.

Under the new arrangement the food bank collects the same morning, before the date runs out, and sorts it within an hour. The bakery has given about 70 kilograms a week since May, slightly less than before, and nothing has been refused.

The manager still thinks the rule is too strict, and he says so every time he calls. He also calls every Tuesday at nine, and last month he brought two boxes of buns baked that morning, which the food bank accepted.

title: Seven Children in the Reading Room
paragraphs: In September, 34 children came to the first Saturday reading session at a library in Liwan. By December the number was seven. The volunteers had prepared more books, not fewer, and none of them could explain the drop.

The programme ran from two to four in the afternoon, with volunteers reading aloud and then helping each child choose a book. Most of the children were between six and nine and came with an older brother or sister.

A volunteer, Mr Xie, began calling the families who had stopped coming. The answers were similar: two o'clock was when younger children sleep, and the walk to the library crossed a road with no crossing guard on Saturdays.

The team moved the session to ten in the morning and asked two parents to wait at the road from half past nine. Attendance rose to nineteen in January and 26 in March, still below the first week but steadier than before.

The library spent 600 yuan on a sign at the road and 200 on mats for children who arrive early. Mr Xie said the first week had been a false success, because a free picture book was given to every child who came through the door.

The programme now has a waiting list of eleven, and the volunteers have stopped counting the first week as a record. "We were measuring the book, not the reading," Mr Xie said. The next change is a second session on Wednesday afternoons.

title: The Tools That Went Home in Pockets
paragraphs: For eight Sundays, a group of volunteers repaired bicycles for free outside a market in Haizhu. They fixed 214 bikes and lost 21 tools, including four spanners that cost 60 yuan each and a pump nobody could find.

The stand began with a box of tools donated by a retired mechanic, Mr Luo, who also taught the first six volunteers how to adjust a brake. They worked from nine to twelve, and most repairs took less than ten minutes.

The losses were not theft in the usual sense. Volunteers lent tools to people who promised to bring them back, and then packed up without counting. One boy borrowed a pump and returned it to a different stand two weeks later.

In November the group started a sign-out sheet with three columns: name, tool and time. It slowed the work, and on busy mornings a queue of nine bikes formed. Two volunteers stopped coming because they found the sheet annoying.

The group now has a rule that no tool leaves the table, and it lends only pumps, which are cheap. Losses fell to two in three months, and the queue is shorter because each owner now pumps the tyres himself.

Mr Luo said the sheet was never about trust, and that it was about remembering, at the end of a long morning, what had been on the table. The first sheet, with its 21 crossed-out lines, is still in his toolbox.

title: Forty Meals and a Cold Bag
paragraphs: A volunteer kitchen in Nansha cooks 40 hot meals every weekday for older people who live alone in the district. In January, one volunteer noticed that the last twelve meals on the route were cold when they arrived.

The route is 11 kilometres and takes about 90 minutes on three scooters. The meals leave at half past ten in paper boxes stacked in a plastic crate. By the time the third scooter reached the last building, the rice was 31 degrees.

The kitchen tried insulated bags, which cost 180 yuan each, and it needed eight. A local shop gave four, and the volunteers raised 720 yuan for the rest by selling used books outside the market on two Sundays.

The bags kept the rice at 52 degrees on the same route, which was better but still below the 60 degrees the kitchen wanted. The route was also too long, and two volunteers had to leave by noon for their own work.
The kitchen split the route in two and asked four more drivers to take one street each. Cooking moved to ten past ten, so the rice left the pot later, and the last meal now arrives at 61 degrees.

The change added a morning shift on Fridays and costs 300 yuan a month in fuel for three scooters and one car. A volunteer said the numbers were useful, but the real change was simpler: nobody had ever asked the drivers what time they had to be somewhere else.

title: The Class on the Fourth Floor
paragraphs: In October, a volunteer group in Panyu advertised a free class to help older people use their phones. Eighteen people signed up at the community centre. On the first morning, two came, and one of them was the wrong person.

The class was on the fourth floor of a building with no lift, and the notice said room 402 in small print at the bottom. Most of the people who signed up were over seventy, and three of them lived alone.

A volunteer called all eighteen. Six had forgotten the date, four said the stairs were too many, and two said their children had told them not to go because of phone fraud. One woman had gone to the building next door.

The group moved the class to a room on the ground floor beside the entrance and put the room number in large letters on the notice. It also asked people to bring a family member to the first session, and eight did.

Eleven people came in November and fourteen in December. The group now runs two classes, one for beginners and one for people who want to learn about payment apps, and it keeps the door open until the last person leaves.

A volunteer said the first advertisement had been written for people who already knew how to find a room. The group now prints notices in 18-point type and reads them aloud to anyone who calls, which takes about ten minutes each.

title: Two Hundred Saplings in July
paragraphs: On 12 July, 200 young trees were planted along a new path in a country park in Conghua by 60 volunteers. By October, 63 of them were alive. The rest had dried out, and about twenty had been eaten by goats.

July was chosen because the volunteers were free then, not because it was a good month for planting. The soil was dry, the saplings had come from a nursery two days before, and there was no shade along the path.
A park worker, Mr Su, had asked for the planting to wait until March. He was overruled because the donation of 200 trees had a date on it and the group wanted to finish before the school term began.

The group watered twice a week through August, carrying 20-litre cans up the path in the heat. It was not enough. In September they counted 92 dead trees and stopped watering the rest, which saved about 40 hours of volunteer time.

In March the group planted 150 trees, with Mr Su choosing both the week and the spot. By June, 138 were alive. The group now writes the planting month into every plan before it accepts a donation of trees.

The donor from last year has given another 150 trees for next March, and Mr Su has asked for a line of shade cloth along the path. The bare line from July is still visible, and the group has decided to leave it as it is, as a warning for next year.

title: Three Tonnes of Clothes in a Corridor
paragraphs: A winter clothes drive at a community centre in Huadu collected 3.1 tonnes of clothing from local families in nine days. Volunteers stacked the bags in a corridor because the store room was full by the third day.

Sorting took three weekends, 22 volunteers and a borrowed van. About 240 kilograms could be worn again. The rest was torn, stained, or single shoes and broken belts, and the centre had expected most of the bags to be useful.

The corridor was 1.4 metres wide and also the building's only fire exit. In the second week a safety officer asked for the bags to be moved within 48 hours. The centre paid 900 yuan for a van to take 1.9 tonnes to a recycling plant.

The centre changed its rules for the next drive. It asked for coats, blankets and shoes only, in pairs, and it put the list on the notice board and in the phone group. Donations fell to 800 kilograms, and 610 of those were usable.

The second drive also needed a store room before it began, which the centre found in a shop that is empty on Sundays. Two volunteers weighed every bag at the door and turned away three that held wet clothes.

A volunteer said the first drive had been a success on paper and a problem in the corridor, and that both were true. The centre now writes the storage plan first, before it prints a single notice asking people to give.

title: The Same Cigarette Ends Every Sunday
paragraphs: Every Sunday morning for five weeks, eleven volunteers from a local group picked up rubbish in a small square in Tianhe. Each week they filled about two kilograms of bags, and each week most of it was cigarette ends.

The group first thought the square was simply dirty, and then they decided to count. In one hour they found 640 cigarette ends, and 410 of them were within five metres of two benches where people played cards.

There was a bin on the north side, 60 metres away, and none near the benches. The volunteers asked the district office for a bin and were told that the square was cleaned twice a day and had no budget for new street furniture.

The group wrote a short report with the count and a map, and sent it with 43 signatures from shops around the square. In June a bin was installed beside the benches, paid for by a shop that sells drinks and snacks.

The next four Sundays produced 0.9 kilograms of rubbish each time, less than half of before. Not all of it was cigarette ends, and there were also bottle caps, paper cups and a broken umbrella that took two people to carry.

A volunteer said the square had not become clean, only cleaner, and that the group still comes every Sunday with gloves and bags. The shop that paid for the bin has asked for a second one near the bus stop, and the office has not answered.

title: Twelve Dogs and One Bag of Sausages
paragraphs: For six Saturdays, 24 volunteers walked dogs from a shelter in Zengcheng. The programme was popular, and by the third week there was a waiting list of 40 people from the town. Then one dog became ill after a walk.

The dog, a seven-year-old brown dog, was sick on a Sunday night and spent two days at a vet. The bill was 680 yuan, and a volunteer had given it three sausages from a bag bought at a shop near the shelter.

The shelter's rule is that visitors bring no food, because many of the dogs are on special diets and some have allergies. The rule was on a poster inside the office, which volunteers passed on their way to the gate but rarely read.

The shelter stopped the programme for three weeks and rewrote the instructions for volunteers. Every volunteer now signs a sheet and listens to a five-minute talk before the first walk, and the waiting list fell from 40 to 17.

Six of the 24 people did not come back after the pause. The programme restarted in October with 12 volunteers and 12 dogs, one for each, and a volunteer stays with the same dog so that both get used to the same person.

The dog recovered and now walks with a volunteer who has come every Saturday since the restart. The manager said the pause had cost the shelter about 3,000 yuan in cancelled donations, and that she would do the same thing again.

title: The Tram That Became a Bus Lane
paragraphs: For sixty-one years a green tram ran along the river in a district west of the city. On the last Sunday of March it made its final trip at ten past five in the afternoon. Forty-one passengers were on board, and the driver had worked the line since 1998.

The tram was slow, and everyone along the street knew it. It shared the road with cars for most of its route and averaged eleven kilometres an hour. A bus on the same street does nineteen. The office said it lost 2.4 million yuan yearly. It carries nine hundred people a day, down from six thousand in 2005.

Ms Xia, who had taken the tram to work for nineteen years, was on the last trip. "I could read two pages between my stop and the office," she said. "The bus shakes too much to read, and it stops on the other side of the road."

Not everyone at the office agreed. Two of the seven members voted against the plan and asked for a trial year with fewer trams. Their report said the bus would add eleven minutes in the morning rush. In April the bus added nine minutes, not eleven.

The rails are still in the road. Workers filled the groove with black rubber so bicycle wheels would not catch. A bus now runs the route every eight minutes. In May the office will count passengers again and publish the number. Ms Xia has bought a folding bicycle and rides it to the second stop.

title: Nine People on the Morning Ferry
paragraphs: The ferry left a fishing village at seven on the first Monday of April, with nine people on board. The wind was cold and the water was flat. Fifteen years ago the same boat carried about a hundred and forty. Most of them were workers going to the factories on the other side.

A new bridge opened in January 2025. The bus over it takes nine minutes instead of thirty-five, and it runs every twenty minutes until eleven. The ferry company kept its old timetable for a year and lost money every month. Its own accounts show 380,000 yuan lost in 2025.

"The boat does not burn much fuel," said Mr Pan, who has steered it for twenty-two years. "But four crew and an engine that needs a part every spring cost more than nine tickets can pay. In March we took in four thousand yuan and spent nineteen."

The company wanted to stop all crossings. The village committee argued that the nearest bus stop is two kilometres from the pier. It also said the road floods for days in summer. In the end they agreed on three crossings a day, at seven, at noon and at five.

On the noon crossing last Tuesday there were two passengers and a crate of vegetables. Mr Pan says he will keep the boat going while the village pays for the diesel. That comes to about nine hundred yuan a month. The new bridge has no footpath, so nobody walks across it.

title: The Footpath That Went Back to Walking
paragraphs: On the first of June, a two-kilometre footpath along the river in Liwan put up twelve signs. The signs say one thing: no electric bikes. Before June, about four hundred e-bikes used the path every morning. They came between seven and nine, when the path is busiest.

The change followed two crashes in eight months. In the second one, an e-bike hit a woman of seventy-one and she stayed in hospital for eleven days. The district then asked six hundred walkers what they wanted. Seventy-eight percent said bikes should leave the path. Only nine wanted them to stay.

Riders objected. "I lose six minutes on every order if I go round by the main road," said Mr Feng, who delivers noodles. "Six minutes, eight times a day. That is my lunch." A group of riders asked for a marked lane at one edge instead of a ban.

For the first month there were no fines, only warnings. Sixty-three riders were stopped in the first week. Fines of fifty yuan began in July, after two warnings. Twice that month someone pulled down a sign at night, and both signs were replaced with heavier posts.

In September the office counted again. Forty e-bikes used the path in the morning peak, and most of them were pushed. The walking count rose from nine hundred to thirteen hundred. Mr Feng now leaves home eight minutes earlier and takes the main road.

title: Two Hundred Metres to the New Entrance
paragraphs: On 12 March the B entrance of a metro station in Yuexiu closed. A new one opened two hundred metres north, at the corner of a smaller street. The old entrance had stood beside a bus stop for sixteen years. Two of its three steps were worn into a shallow curve.

The building above it was going to be rebuilt, and the escalator inside needed replacing. Moving the entrance cost 4.6 million yuan and took fourteen months. Workers cut a passage through a wall 1.2 metres thick. They did it at night, between the last and the first train. The station stayed open the whole time.

"I have walked the same way for eleven years," said Ms Gao, who works at a hospital three stops away. "Now I come up in a street where I do not know a single shop. I turned the wrong way on Monday, again on Tuesday, and once more on Friday."

The three shops nearest the old entrance lost customers. The noodle shop said its lunch trade fell by a third in April, and the owners wrote to the district twice. The office offered to move the bus stop closer. The road there is too narrow for a shelter.

By June the station counted 19,000 people a day at the new entrance. That is about the same as before. The noodle shop put a paper sign on the old corner, with an arrow and four words. By July its lunch trade was back to about ninety percent.

title: Six Minutes Longer, Every Order
paragraphs: Mr Tan starts work at half past nine and used to finish about fifty orders a day. His scooter stopped at the front plaza of an office building. He ran in with the bag and was back on the road in four minutes flat. In April all of that changed.

The building manager banned bikes from the plaza after a scooter hit a six-year-old child in February. The child needed four stitches and still has the scar. Riders now park in a marked bay behind the building, with twenty-four spaces. They walk the last eighty metres, past the goods lift.

The walk takes five minutes when the lift is free. It takes nine when the lift is busy with boxes. Mr Tan is paid 4.2 yuan an order. A day of forty-four orders instead of fifty costs him about twenty-five yuan. He also bought a smaller bag for the turnstile.

"I am not against walking," he said, waiting for the lift with two bags of rice. "I am against the clock. The app does not know I parked eighty metres away, and the customer does not know either. They see a map with a little bike on it."

After six weeks the building added a second rack for twenty bikes. It also gave riders a pass for the goods lift. The delivery company added three minutes to the estimated time for that address. Mr Tan is back to forty-eight orders, and the child's mother has thanked two riders.

title: Forty-Two Steps Instead of Six
paragraphs: In February a zebra crossing on a six-lane road in Haizhu closed. A footbridge opened forty metres away. The bridge has forty-two steps on each side and a ramp that runs ninety metres. The road below carries about 42,000 vehicles a day. It is the busiest road in the district.

The crossing had been the scene of eleven injuries in three years, three of them serious. The district said drivers coming off the bridge could not see it in the morning sun. The bridge cost 6.8 million yuan. It was finished four months late, because of a water pipe.

Not everyone uses it. Ms Zhen, who is seventy-four, goes to the market on the other side every morning. "Six steps or forty-two, that is not a small difference when your knee hurts," she said. She now takes a bus one stop, which costs two yuan and twelve minutes.

In the first month the bridge counted 1,500 people a day. About 2,100 had used the zebra crossing. Sixty or seventy people a day still crossed at the old place. In March the district put up a fence, and a section of it was cut twice.

The district added two benches at the top of the bridge and a handrail on the ramp. A lift will not come before 2027, because the estimate is 1.8 million yuan. A nurse at a clinic nearby said three older patients mentioned the bridge in one week. None of them mentioned the view.

title: The Ticket Window That Closed in March
paragraphs: On 3 March the ticket office at a small railway station in Panyu closed. Its two windows became one machine and a help desk. Last year the windows sold thirty-eight percent of the station's tickets, about 260 a day. Most of those buyers were over sixty.

The machine took five months to install. The old windows had no queue most mornings. The floor of the hall had to be strengthened, and a new cable run under it. Three clerks were moved to other stations. One stayed at the help desk, where she also answers questions about the machine.

"The machine asks me four questions and gives me twenty seconds for each," said Mr Liang. He is sixty-eight, walks with a stick, and visits his sister twice a month. "I need a minute. The young man behind me said nothing, but I could hear him breathing."

The station then put a table beside the machine. A volunteer helps there from nine to eleven, the busiest hours. In April the volunteers helped 214 people, and about 160 of them were over sixty. The machine itself broke down twice, both times on a Monday.

By June, eighty-two percent of tickets were bought on phones or at the machine. The queue at the help desk had fallen from twenty people to six. Mr Liang now asks his daughter to buy his ticket the night before. He still arrives forty minutes early and sits by the window.

title: One Bus, Two Schools, Twenty Minutes Earlier
paragraphs: In September two schools in Zengcheng began sharing one school bus. Route A had thirty-one students, and route B had nineteen. The company said two buses for fifty students lost 4,600 yuan a month. It gave the schools a choice: one bus or no bus. Both schools start at ten to eight.

The new route has eleven stops and runs 14.2 kilometres. It leaves the first stop at 6:35 instead of 6:55. Students must be at the road five minutes before that. The bus has fifty-six seats and a rule that the front four seats are for the youngest.

"My son gets up at six now," said Mr Luo, whose son is in grade 7. "In October he fell asleep in the first class three times, and the teacher called me. I told her he was on the bus at twenty past six, and she was quiet. Then she said sorry."

In the first month the bus reached school on time on ninety-two percent of mornings. It was late four times, three of them at a level crossing. A goods train passes there at about 7:10. Three families left the bus and now drive, which adds forty cars to the gate.

In November the company moved the first pickup eight minutes later by cutting two stops. The six students who used those stops now walk three hundred metres to a main road. The bus reaches school at 7:38. Mr Luo's son gets up at a quarter past six and has not slept in class since.

title: The Bike Lane That Lasted Five Months
paragraphs: On 8 April workers painted a bike lane 1.9 kilometres long on the right side of a main road. The lane took one of the four car lanes in Tianhe. It was a trial, planned for six months. There were white posts at each junction and a green strip at the bus stops.

In the first month, 1,100 cyclists a day used the lane. About 300 had ridden in the bus lane before. Cars in the three remaining lanes slowed. The morning trip from the roundabout to the river went from eighteen minutes to twenty-six. The bus company said its buses were late by four minutes.

Support was split. Nine hundred people signed a paper to keep the lane, and twelve hundred signed one to remove it. "I rode to work in twenty-two minutes and did not look behind me once," said Ms Wen. "That is worth something, and nobody put it in the report."

The report counted cars, bus times and five junctions, but not the cyclists. Two bus stops had to be moved forty metres. A shop owner said his morning deliveries were blocked by the posts. In September the district voted five to two to remove the lane.

The paint came off in two nights, and the posts went into a truck. The cycling count fell back to 260 in October. The district will try again on a wider road in 2027, with a separate path. Ms Wen now takes the bus, which takes thirty-one minutes.

title: The Bus That Is Too Wide for the Lane
paragraphs: For eighteen years a minibus with nineteen seats ran from a village to the town, six times a day. In May the company replaced it with a bus of thirty-five seats. The old minibus had failed its yearly inspection. A new one of the same size would have cost 260,000 yuan.

The new bus is 2.5 metres wide. The lane into the village is 3.1 metres at its narrowest point, between a brick wall and a ditch. The driver tried the lane twice. On the second try the mirror touched the wall. After that the bus stopped at the main road, seven hundred metres short.

"I drove that lane for eleven years in a smaller bus," said Mr Qiu, who now waits at the main road. "This is a good bus. It is warm, it is quiet, and the door is low. It is just the wrong bus for this road. Nobody asked the road."

For six weeks the village had no bus in it. Older residents walked to the main road, and two of them wrote to the company. The company said a small bus costs 1,900 yuan a day to run. It carries about twelve people, and the village would have to pay the difference.

In July they agreed on a simple arrangement. The big bus runs to the main road, and a village van meets it there. A retired teacher drives the van, three trips a day at two yuan. It holds eight. The ditch was filled in September, and the big bus will be tested again in spring.

title: Forty More Minutes of Sleep
paragraphs: In March a grade 8 class in Baiyun ran a four-week experiment with one rule. Lights went out at half past ten, and there was no homework after nine. The forty-one students wrote two numbers on a card each morning. They wrote the time they went to bed and the time they got up.

In the first week the class averaged seven hours and ten minutes of sleep. By the fourth week it was seven hours and fifty, which is forty minutes more. Ms Xia moved the last homework check to the next morning. Nobody had a reason to sit up late after that.

Eleven students could not change their evenings. Two shared a room with a younger brother, and three helped in a family shop until ten. Six said the building was too noisy before eleven. The class stopped counting those eleven in the weekly average, which made the numbers look better.

"I did not feel different in the morning," said a boy named Zhou. "I felt different in the fourth class. In March I read the question three times and still did not know it. In April I read it once, and I was still there."

The class also counted how many students finished homework after nine. That number fell from twenty-two to four, mostly because the phones were in the box. The rule stayed for another month, but the cards stopped in June. Most of them were being filled in during the break, from memory.

title: Six Grams Less in Every Bottle
paragraphs: From the first of April, the canteen of a school in Liwan changed its drinks. The sweet tea it sold had eleven grams of sugar in every hundred millilitres. The new one has five. The cola did not change, but it moved behind the counter, where a student must ask for it.

The kitchen tried fourteen mixes over two months. A hundred and twenty students tasted them without labels. The chosen mix scored 6.4 out of ten, against 8.1 for the old drink. Sales fell from three hundred bottles a day to 190 in the first week. By May they were back to 260.

Not everyone was pleased. About thirty students began buying the old drink from a shop outside the gate and bringing it in. The school could not stop that. The shop, when asked, moved the sweet tea to its back shelf but kept selling it. The gate is open.

"I know it is better for me," said a grade 8 girl, holding the new bottle. "But at four o'clock, after sport, I want the one that tastes like the old one. This one tastes like water with a leaf in it. I still drink it, so maybe that is the point."

At the end of term the kitchen weighed what it used. It had gone from sixty-two kilograms of sugar a week to thirty-four. The money saved paid for a fruit counter beside the drinks fridge. The fruit sells about ninety bags a day, and the sweet tea is still second.

title: Three Weeks Without Screens After Nine
paragraphs: On 2 March, thirty-four students in a grade 8 class in Haizhu agreed to one rule. For three weeks there would be no screens after nine in the evening. Phones went into a shoe box in the corridor at 8:55. They came back at 6:30 the next morning, and the box had no lock.

Each student wrote down the time they turned off the light. They also wrote how long they thought they lay awake. In the first week they reported forty-one minutes on average. In the third week the number was twenty-eight. Nine students said they had stopped looking at the clock.

Seven students quit before the end. Three needed a phone for a group project, and two said a parent refused the box. One used a tablet instead and did not count it as a screen. The class argued for a whole lesson about whether a tablet counts. Most of them decided that it does.

"The first three nights were the worst," said the class monitor, a girl named He. "I lay there and my hand kept looking for the phone on the table. It was not there, and my hand still went. By the fifth night my hand stopped going."

The three weeks ended on 23 March. Nineteen of the thirty-four kept the rule for another month. The box is still in the corridor, though nobody locks it now. The class did not measure sleep again, so nobody can say whether the good nights lasted. He now reads a paper book until ten.

title: The Checklist at the Clinic Door
paragraphs: In January a clinic in Liwan put a nurse at the door with a paper list. The list had six questions. Before that, patients walked straight to the desk and sat down. The clinic sees about two hundred and ten people on a Monday, mostly between eight and ten.

The list asks about fever in the last three days, a cough and recent travel. It also asks about illness at home and work in a kitchen. The sixth question is simple: have you taken anything for this today? That one was added in the second week. Nobody liked it at first.

The queue reached the street on the first Monday. The nurse, Ms Tang, takes about forty seconds with each person. That is two hours and twenty minutes of her day. A second nurse was added at nine o'clock, which costs the clinic four thousand yuan a month.

"I did not want it," said Dr Feng, who has worked there for nine years. "I thought it would slow us down and make people angry. In February we found four cases of the same stomach illness from one kitchen in two days. After that I stopped arguing with the nurse."

The clinic counted two things in March. Eleven patients with fever were moved to a separate room, against two in December. The average wait rose from twelve minutes to seventeen. From June the list drops to four questions, because fewer people have coughs in summer.

title: The Month the Gate Was Quiet
paragraphs: On the first of May a school in Panyu began a month of walking. Every student who came on foot got a card. A shop two hundred metres from the gate stamped it between 7:10 and 7:45. The school printed nine hundred cards and gave out six hundred and forty in the first week.

In April, teachers counted the cars dropping students off. There were two hundred and ten on a normal morning, and two hundred and sixty on a rainy one. The road outside is narrow, and the last fifty metres often took four minutes. The three classes with the most stamps would win an extra PE lesson.

In the first week three hundred and eighty students walked, against about a hundred and fifty in April. The car count at the gate fell to a hundred and fifty. Two teachers stood at the corner with a clicker. A grade 7 class led for eleven days, until a grade 8 class passed it.

"I get up seven minutes earlier," said a girl named Tang, whose card had nineteen stamps. "My father drives to work anyway, so he takes my bag and I walk. The bag was the reason he drove me to the gate. Now it is not, and he leaves without me."

Then the rain came on 19 May, and stayed for nine days. The stamps fell to ninety a day, and the shop closed early twice because nobody came. The month ended with 214 cards full. The car count is back at 195. The school will run it again in September, with a roof over the stamping place.

title: Two Extra Sinks by the Canteen
paragraphs: In February a school in Tianhe put two extra sinks outside the canteen door. Soap and paper towels were put beside them. The school has 1,100 students, and before that all of them shared six sinks. The nearest one to the fourth floor was a tap in a toilet.

The nurse, Ms Deng, had been keeping a record. In November, sixty-three students went home with stomach illness. Most of them were in two classes on the fourth floor. She took the record to the head teacher with a photograph of the corridor tap.

The sinks cost 8,700 yuan and took a week to install. The pipes were run from the kitchen wall. For two weeks a teacher stood at the door for the first ten minutes of lunch. She said one sentence to everybody who passed: soap, then twenty seconds.

One teacher said at the meeting that students wash their hands anyway. He said the money would be better spent on the roof. The nurse answered with a count. On the first day she watched two hundred students go in, and forty-one used soap. On the ninth day, a hundred and fifty-eight did.

In April the nurse compared the two months. Twelve students went home with stomach illness, against sixty-three in November. She says the number is too small to prove anything and the weather was different. The school kept the sinks and put soap on the shopping list, forty bottles a month.

title: Four Floors, No Lift, One Month
paragraphs: On 6 April, twenty-eight teachers and ninety-six students at a school in Yuexiu agreed to use the stairs. The building has six floors and one lift. The lift was put in in 2009 and broke down fourteen times last year. Twice it stopped with somebody inside, once for forty minutes.

The rule was simple. Anyone going up two floors or fewer took the stairs. The lift was kept for the injured, for food trolleys and for visitors. Four students stood at the lift door from 7:30 to 8:00 with a clicker. The numbers went on a paper chart by the stairs.

Before April the lift made about two hundred and forty trips a day. In the first week it made ninety-six. By the fourth week it made seventy. The repair company came twice that month, once for the door. The second visit was for a button pressed too hard by somebody in a hurry.

"I carry two bags of books up to the fifth floor," said Mr Su, who teaches history. "On the first day I reached my class out of breath and the students laughed. By the third week I was not out of breath, and they had stopped laughing."

Six people with knee problems were given a paper card for the lift. The month ended, the chart stayed on the wall, and the clickers went back to the sports room. The lift now makes about a hundred and twenty trips a day. Nobody has been stuck in it since May.

title: Breakfast at Seven Fifteen
paragraphs: On 20 February a school in Huangpu opened a small room beside the canteen. It opens at a quarter past seven and sells breakfast for three yuan. For that money a student gets porridge, an egg, a bun and a cup of soy milk. The room has forty-eight chairs and two bins.

The idea came from a survey of three hundred grade 8 students. Seventy-eight of them came to school without breakfast at least twice a week. A head teacher also remembered a boy who fainted in a PE lesson in December. He had eaten nothing since the night before.

In the first week the room sold sixty breakfasts a day. By April it sold a hundred and ninety. The kitchen cooks two hundred and throws away about twelve. Each meal costs 3.4 yuan to make and sells for three. The school loses about eighty yuan a day and pays from the lunch income.

"I used to buy a bag of chips at the shop on the corner," said a boy named Wu. "It cost four yuan, and by ten o'clock I was hungry again. The porridge is boring and there is never enough sugar. But I am not hungry at ten o'clock."

The school measured one thing only: students who went to the nurse before ten, saying they felt sick. In March it was twenty-three. In the same month last year it was fifty-one. The room closes at 7:50 exactly. Fourteen students were late for class in April because they came for a second bun.

title: One Bottle Before the Second Class
paragraphs: In March, forty students in a grade 7 class in Zengcheng put a bottle on the corner of the desk. Each bottle held half a litre. They were asked to finish it before the second class. The school bought the bottles at six yuan each and wrote a name on every lid.

The teacher, Ms Qiu, took the idea from the nurse's book. In February, seventeen students in her class went to the nurse with a headache. Eleven of them had drunk nothing since getting up. There is a water fountain in the corridor, but the break is eight minutes.

In the first week nine students finished the bottle. By the third week thirty-four did. Two students had to leave the class in the middle of a lesson. One teacher complained, so Ms Qiu changed the rule. Half the bottle before the second class, and half before lunch.

"I did not know I was thirsty," said a girl named Luo. "I thought a headache was a Tuesday thing, because I always get one on Tuesday. Now I think it was a nine o'clock thing. It happened on Tuesday because Tuesday is when we have double maths."

In April six students went to the nurse with a headache, against seventeen in February. The nurse said the weather had changed and April is always easier. Ms Qiu kept the bottles but stopped counting them. In June the fountain was moved to the other end of the corridor, outside her room.

title: Fruit at Ten O'Clock
paragraphs: On the first of April a school in Baiyun began selling fruit at the tuck shop window. For two yuan a student gets a small bag of cut pineapple, guava or orange. Before that the window sold only fried snacks and sweet drinks. It opened at seven in the morning.

The change came with the shop's new contract. The school added one condition. From ten to twenty past ten, the window sells fruit and nothing else. The owner, Mr Mai, said he would lose money. He sold about a hundred and twenty bags of chips a week, most of them in that break.

In the first week he sold ninety bags of fruit a day. Chips fell to forty a week. A bag of fruit costs him 1.1 yuan, so he makes ninety cents on it. A bag of chips makes 1.2. He told the school he was working longer hours for less money.

"I argued for two weeks," Mr Mai said, cutting a pineapple on a board. "Then I saw the same boy buy pineapple four days in a row. He used to buy chips every day and never looked at anything else. I still do not like the maths, but I like that."

By June the window sold a hundred and forty bags of fruit a day. Mr Mai had bought a second fridge for twenty more. Two students were caught eating fruit in class, so the rule became: eat it at the window. The chips did not disappear. They moved to after four and still sell about seventy a week.
